Dragon Ball built a world. Why is its largest physical destination outside Japan?

A new television edit has returned Goku to the beginning of Super. Tokyo has opened the world’s first permanent Dragon Ball store. Saudi Arabia is building something more than a thousand times larger. Together, they reveal how differently Japan and the world value the same imaginary universe.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published October 20, 2026, 9:30 p.m. JST

On Sunday night in Japan, a familiar god arrived again. Beerus woke from a long sleep, dreamed of a Super Saiyan God, and set a route toward Earth. Fans knew the destination because versions of this story had already appeared in a 2013 film and the opening arc of Dragon Ball Super in 2015. Yet Dragon Ball Super: Beerus, which premiered on October 11, 2026, is not merely the old broadcast placed back on television.

Official descriptions call it an “enhanced edition.” The production combines newly created and redrawn footage, reconstructed story material, updated visual expression and a closer relationship to Akira Toriyama’s manga version. It has a new opening, “ONOGAMI” by MEGATERA・ZERO, and a new ending, “Kan Peki No Peki” by VK Blanka. Fuji TV broadcasts it Sundays at 11:15 p.m. JST; Crunchyroll began international streaming on October 11, with other services and territories following on different schedules.

1984Akira Toriyama’s manga begins in Weekly Shonen Jump.
250m+Manga copies sold worldwide, according to Toei Animation.
500,000m²+Planned area of Qiddiya’s Dragon Ball theme park.

So is Beerus a new series?

Yes as a television production; no as a wholly new chapter of the story. That distinction explains both the excitement and the frustration around its opening episodes. It is best understood as a rebuilt route through the beginning of Dragon Ball Super: the Beerus material is familiar, but the pacing, images and story emphasis are being reconsidered.

The first episodes make the proposition visible. Scenes are redrawn or expanded, the visual finish is more consistent, and material can align more closely with the manga rather than simply repeating the 2015 television cut. For newcomers, it is intended to become a cleaner entry into Super. For longtime viewers, the attraction lies in comparison: which joke was shortened, which fight beat gained weight, and which piece of Toriyama’s characterization returned?

The surprise is that Dragon Ball’s current “new” television event is an act of preservation. Japan is rebuilding the doorway to an existing world while Saudi Arabia prepares to build that world at architectural scale.

Official Dragon Ball Super: Beerus Super Surge trailer, embedded from the Dragon Ball official channel. The footage shows the enhanced production; copyright remains with the listed Dragon Ball rights holders.

What viewers are actually saying

Online reaction is not a scientific poll. People who post in anime communities are self-selecting, English-language discussion misses Japan and many other markets, and the loudest comment is not necessarily the typical viewer. Within those limits, the early response shows a clear split.

One group welcomes a definitive version. Viewers praise cleaner animation, added material and the chance to repair an opening arc often compared unfavorably with the film Battle of Gods. Some call it a “Super Kai” approach: not a replacement for future stories, but a tighter and more attractive path through material that new viewers still need.

Another group expected forward motion. Their question is blunt: after years of waiting, why return to Beerus instead of animating later manga arcs? International viewers have also complained about uneven platform dates and the absence of an immediately available English dub. Those objections matter because they reveal the burden of a forty-year franchise. Restoration can delight one generation while feeling like delay to another.

The fairest reading is not that fans love it or hate it. They are negotiating what “new” should mean. Better craft, restored scenes and a new weekly conversation are real changes. So is the fact that the central plot is already known.

Forty-two volumes became generations

Toriyama began Dragon Ball in 1984, drawing on the Chinese classic Journey to the West, martial-arts cinema, comedy and adventure. The original manga ran until 1995 and was collected in 42 volumes. Toei’s first television series, Dragon Ball (1986–1989), follows young Goku’s comic search for the seven wish-granting spheres. Dragon Ball Z (1989–1996) expands the scale to Saiyan heritage, planetary threats and transformations that became global visual language.

Dragon Ball GT (1996–1997) continued as an anime-original sequel. Dragon Ball Z Kai (2009–2015) recut and remastered Z with a faster structure. Dragon Ball Super began in 2015, bringing Beerus, Whis, multiple universes and new forms into the main modern continuity. The theatrical branch includes Battle of Gods, Resurrection ‘F’, Dragon Ball Super: Broly and Super Hero. Dragon Ball Daima, launched in 2024, became Toriyama’s final major animated project after his death that year.

1984–95Original manga
1986–96Dragon Ball + Z
1996–97GT
2009–15Z Kai
2015–18Super
2024–25Daima
2026–Super: Beerus

That list still understates the phenomenon. Games, toys, cards, films and live events let people enter at different ages and in different countries. Toei Animation reports more than 250 million manga copies sold worldwide and decades of continuous European broadcasting. Dragon Ball is not simply exported Japanese animation; it is a shared childhood memory whose language—powering up, fusion, collecting seven objects—can cross borders without translation.

The world’s first store fits inside Tokyo Station

Dragon Ball Store Tokyo opened on November 14, 2025, on the first floor of First Avenue Tokyo Station. The official site calls it the world’s first dedicated Dragon Ball store. It sells exclusive merchandise and uses interior decoration to create a concentrated encounter with the franchise. It is one minute from JR Tokyo Station’s Yaesu North Exit and normally operates from 10:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m., following First Avenue’s hours.

The location is intelligent. Tokyo Station connects long-distance visitors, commuters, airports and the character-shopping district below and around the station. A fan can encounter Dragon Ball between a Shinkansen arrival and dinner. Toei Animation has told investors that the store is not only about direct profit: it is meant to strengthen engagement and the long-term value of the intellectual property.

But it is still a store. Its success proves that Japan sees value in a permanent official address, not that Japan has built a destination equal to the imaginative size of the work. For visitors, practical reality matters: the shop is compact, limited goods can change, and crowd-control measures may apply during launches. Check the official store site before making it the center of a trip.

Saudi Arabia is making the opposite bet

At Qiddiya City near Riyadh, the planned Dragon Ball theme park exceeds 500,000 square meters. Qiddiya Investment Company describes seven themed zones corresponding to the seven Dragon Balls, more than 30 rides and attractions, five headline attractions, themed hotels and recognizable places including Kame House, Capsule Corporation and Beerus’ Planet. A signature Shenron roller coaster is planned to rise 70 meters.

This is not a fan rumor or an unlicensed proposal. Qiddiya and Toei Animation announced the project in 2024 as an authorized collaboration. It forms part of Saudi Arabia’s wider effort to build tourism and entertainment industries. The park does not yet have a confirmed public opening date, so concept images and attraction counts describe the plan, not a finished experience.

The scale changes the economics. A shop monetizes products and foot traffic. A destination can sell travel, hotels, food, repeat visits, events and the feeling of standing inside a story. It can also fail at far greater cost. Qiddiya’s advantage is not that Saudi Arabia understands Dragon Ball better than Japan; it is that a state-backed development can assemble land, capital, transport and a tourism strategy around one enormous bet.

Why has Japan not done the same?

The tempting answer is that Japan lacks imagination. The evidence points to a more complicated constraint. Japan’s most valuable character worlds are divided among creators, publishers, animation studios, broadcasters, toy and game companies, music companies and local operators. That system is excellent at distributing risk and producing many forms of media. It can make a permanent, unified destination harder to negotiate.

Land is another difference. A 500,000-square-meter project near central Tokyo would face extraordinary land costs, fragmented ownership, planning rules and neighborhood impacts. Regional Japan has space, but then transport, hotels, staffing and year-round demand become the problem. Seasonal pop-ups and compact stores are easier to approve, refresh and close if demand changes.

Japan is also not empty of ambitious character attractions. Universal Studios Japan has built major anime collaborations; Ghibli Park uses landscape and atmosphere rather than thrill-ride scale; Nijigen no Mori turns works such as Naruto and Dragon Quest into outdoor experiences; Sanrio Puroland and Nintendo’s theme-park worlds prove that domestic IP can anchor physical places. The gap is therefore specific: Japan has few permanent, large-scale destinations dedicated to a single manga-anime universe with Dragon Ball’s international reach.

That gap is an opportunity, but not an automatic financial victory. A Japanese Dragon Ball destination would need a region that benefits from multi-day stays, fast transport, multilingual operations, heat and rain planning, changing attractions and a rights structure able to make decisions for decades. It should not merely copy Qiddiya. Japan’s strongest version could connect animation craft, manga history, training games, food, landscapes and limited events—a place that explains how the world was made while letting visitors enter it.

Japan does not need to prove it can make worlds. Dragon Ball already proved that. The unanswered question is whether Japan can organize land, rights and long-term capital around the worlds it makes.

The next transformation is physical

Dragon Ball Super: Beerus looks backward in order to rebuild an entry point. The Tokyo store gives the franchise a permanent but compact home. Qiddiya takes the most expansive route, translating seven fictional objects into seven real zones. These are not competing versions of the same business. They are three answers to the question of how a forty-year story remains present.

Fans watching the enhanced anime are debating whether restored history counts as something new. The physical projects make the same debate concrete. A shop preserves and sells symbols. A theme park asks people to cross borders and inhabit them. If Japan wants more of the tourism, jobs and cultural gravity created by its stories, the next step is not another temporary photo spot. It is the difficult coordination required to let an imaginary world occupy real space for a generation.

Until then, the contrast remains almost cinematic. In Tokyo, the world’s first official Dragon Ball store sits inside the country’s busiest rail gateway. Near Riyadh, desert land is being prepared for a Shenron seventy meters high.
